lesson.title: Costs and the best output

steps.headline: Costs that move and costs that don't

lead.text: Costs fall into two kinds. A fixed cost is one the firm pays whatever it makes, such as rent. A variable cost grows with output, such as paper, flour or wages paid by the hour. Adding the two gives total cost, the full bill for a given amount of output.

Take a print shop that pays £50 rent a day and spends £1 on paper and ink for every poster. If it prints nothing, its total cost is still the £50 of rent. If it prints 20 posters, the variable cost is 20 × £1 = £20 and the total cost is £50 + £20 = £70.

The difference matters when a firm makes decisions. The rent has to be paid whatever the firm chooses, but each extra poster brings a cost with it. A sensible choice about how much to print looks at the costs the choice itself changes, and the next two screens turn that idea into two measures.

The first measure is the cost of a typical unit. Average total cost is total cost divided by the number of units made. Take a workshop that pays £36 rent a day. Other costs climb as the room fills, so making q units adds q² on top of the rent. Total cost is then TC = 36 + q².

Two units cost 36 + 4 = £40 in total, an average of £20 each. Six units cost 36 + 36 = £72, an average of £12. Twelve units cost 36 + 144 = £180, an average of £15. The cost per unit falls and then rises.

afterFigure.text: The fall comes from the rent. With only 2 units each one carries £18 of it, and with 6 units each carries £6. The rise comes from crowding, which makes every unit beyond the sixth cost more to squeeze in. The two effects balance at 6 units, where the average is lowest.
The figure shows this workshop and one with £100 rent. The higher rent pushes the lowest point to a larger output.

lead.text: Take the bakery from the start of the lesson. Each loaf also uses £2 of flour, and the rent is shared across the loaves baked that day.

Average cost smooths everything into one number per unit. A firm deciding whether to make one more unit needs something sharper. Marginal cost is the extra cost of making that one more unit, which is the change in total cost when output goes up by one.

In the workshop, going from 5 to 6 units lifts total cost from 36 + 25 = £61 to £72, so the sixth unit has a marginal cost of £11. The seventh takes it from £72 to £85, which is £13. Marginal cost rises with output here, and the line MC = 2q runs through the middle of those two figures, at £12 for 6 units. This course uses MC = 2q for the workshop.

afterFigure.text: Marginal cost and average cost are linked. If the next unit costs less than the average so far, adding it pulls the average down. If it costs more, it pulls the average up. At 2 units the marginal cost is about £4 against an average of £20, so the average is being pulled down. At 12 units it is about £24 against £15, so the average is being pulled up.
The average stops falling at the output where marginal cost has risen to meet it. For the workshop that is 6 units, where marginal cost is £12 and so is the average.

lead.text: Marginal cost is read from a table of total costs by subtracting each total from the one after it.

steps.headline: A workshop pays £400 rent, with variable cost q². At what output is average total cost lowest?

workedSteps.text: Write marginal cost and average total cost.
Average cost is lowest where marginal cost meets it.

steps.headline: With £100 rent and variable cost q², find the output where average total cost is lowest.

workedSteps.text: Write marginal cost and average total cost.

steps.headline: How much to make at a given price

lead.text: Now the choice itself. A firm in a very large market cannot move the price by changing its own output, so it takes the price as given. Such a firm is called a price-taker. Every extra unit it sells brings in exactly the market price, and the revenue that one more unit adds is called marginal revenue. For a price-taker, marginal revenue equals the price.

The rule follows from comparing marginal revenue with marginal cost. While a unit adds more revenue than cost, making it raises profit. Once it adds more cost than revenue, making it lowers profit. Marginal cost rises with output, so there is a single best output, where marginal cost has just risen to the price.

afterFigure.text: Try it on the £36 workshop at a price of £20. Setting 20 = 2q gives q = 10. Revenue is 20 × 10 = £200 and total cost is 36 + 100 = £136, so profit is £64. A unit beyond 10 would add about £22 of cost for £20 of revenue, and a unit short of 10 would leave money on the table. The figure marks the best output at two prices.

lead.text: The same test works on a single unit. Compare what the unit adds to revenue with what it adds to cost.

reveal.text: Below 15 units the next unit adds more revenue than cost; beyond 15 it adds less. That is the marginal rule from the start of the course, applied to output.

lead.text: The workshop with £100 rent has marginal cost MC = 2q and now sells at £30 a unit. Choose the output that makes the most profit.

steps.headline: When the price will not cover the rent

lead.text: A falling price tests the rule. At a lower price the best output is smaller, and revenue may no longer cover total cost, which leaves the firm with a loss. The natural question is whether it should close.

In the short run the rent has to be paid whether or not the firm makes anything, so closing does not avoid it. Take the £36 workshop at a price of £8. Setting 8 = 2q gives q = 4. Revenue is 8 × 4 = £32 and total cost is 36 + 16 = £52, a loss of £20. Closing would lose the whole £36 of rent.

afterFigure.text: The comparison shows why it carries on. The £32 of revenue covers the £16 of variable cost and puts £16 towards the rent, which cuts the loss from £36 to £20. A firm should keep producing while revenue covers its variable costs, and should close only if the price falls so low that it does not. The next question puts the other workshop in the same position.

reveal.text: A loss of £36 is still better than shutting down, which would lose the whole £100 of rent. In the short run the firm keeps producing.

lead.text: The market price falls to £16. Find the best output again, and then see whether it still pays.

lesson.orientation: Separate fixed, variable, average and marginal cost, and choose output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A bakery pays £60 rent every day, whether it bakes ten loaves or a hundred. Flour is different, because every extra loaf needs more of it. So a day's baking costs two kinds of money, one that never moves and one that grows with every loaf.

That mix gives the cost of each loaf an odd shape. Bake only a few and every loaf carries a large share of the rent. Bake many and the rent is spread thin, until the kitchen is so crowded that squeezing in one more loaf starts to cost a lot.

So far in this course each market came with a supply equation already written. This lesson opens up the firm behind it. It separates the kinds of cost, finds the output at which a unit is cheapest to make, and then uses the cost of one extra unit to decide how much to make when the market price is fixed.

intro.promise: By the end you'll separate fixed, average and marginal cost, and pick the output that makes a price-taking firm the most profit.

recap.keyIdea: Average total cost is the cost per unit; marginal cost is the cost of one more. A price-taking firm makes the most profit where price equals marginal cost.

blocks.text: The bakery's average cost came to £4 a loaf at 30 loaves. For the workshop with £100 rent, the cost per unit bottomed out at 10 units and profit peaked at 15 units, earning £125. At a price of £16 the firm lost £36 but still beat shutting down.

recap.nextHook: Every firm in this lesson took its price from the market. The next lesson looks at a firm with no rivals, which has to choose its price and so changes the answer.

questions.prompt: A firm's total cost is TC = 100 + q², where £100 is fixed. What is average total cost at q = 5, in pounds?
hints: Average total cost is total cost divided by output.
Find total cost at that output first.
Divide by the number of units.
questions.onCorrect: £25. Total cost is 100 + 25 = 125; divide by 5 units.

misconceptions.feedback: That is total cost. Divide by the output.
That is the output, not the cost per unit.
That shares only the rent over 5 units. The other cost counts too.

questions.prompt: Output with the lowest average cost
hints: Average cost falls while the next unit costs less than the average.
The lowest point is where marginal cost equals average total cost.
Set the two expressions equal and solve for q.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ATC is lowest where MC = ATC: 2q = 100/q + q gives q² = 100, so q = 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10 units. Where MC meets ATC, average cost stops falling.

misconceptions.feedback: That is q squared. Take the square root.
That is the average cost at the lowest point, not the output.

questions.prompt: A competitive firm with MC = 2q sells at a market price of £30. What output maximises its profit?
hints: A price-taker's marginal revenue equals the price.
Produce while the next unit's revenue covers its marginal cost.
Solve price = 2q.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Marginal revenue is the £30 price; 30 = 2q gives q = 15.

questions.onCorrect: 15 units. A price-taker produces until marginal cost rises to meet the price.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the slope. Divide the price by the slope instead.
That is the price, not the output.

questions.prompt: A firm has total cost TC = 100 + q² and sells 15 units at £30 each. What is its profit, in pounds?
hints: Profit is total revenue minus total cost.
Revenue is price times quantity.
Total cost includes the fixed £100.
questions.onCorrect: £125. Revenue less total cost, rent included.

misconceptions.feedback: That is revenue. Subtract total cost.
That is total cost. Subtract it from revenue.

questions.prompt: Total cost is £50 at 0 units, £70 at 1, £85 at 2, £105 at 3 and £135 at 4. What is the marginal cost of the third unit, in pounds?
hints: Marginal cost is the change in total cost from one more unit.
Compare total cost at 2 units and at 3 units.
Subtract the smaller total from the larger.
questions.onCorrect: £20. Marginal cost is the change in total cost from one more unit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total cost at three units. Marginal cost is the change from the unit before.
That is the average cost at three units. Marginal cost is only the extra for the third.
That is the extra cost of the fourth unit. Look at the third.

questions.prompt: A competitive firm sells at £50 and its marginal cost is MC = 10 + 2q. What output maximises profit?
hints: Set price equal to marginal cost.
Move the constant to one side.
Divide by the slope of the marginal cost line.
questions.onCorrect: 20 units. Set price equal to marginal cost, then solve.

misconceptions.feedback: That is price minus the constant. Divide by the slope as well.
That ignores the constant in marginal cost.

questions.prompt: A bakery pays £60 rent a day whatever it bakes, and each loaf also costs £2 in flour. On a day it bakes 30 loaves, what is the average cost per loaf, in pounds?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Total cost is 60 + 30 × 2 = £120. Divide by 30 loaves: £4.

hints: Find the day's total cost: rent and flour together.
Flour costs the same for each loaf, but the rent is paid once.
Divide the total cost by the number of loaves.
questions.onCorrect: £4. The rent is shared across every loaf, so each loaf's average cost is more than its flour.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the flour only. The rent is part of the day's cost.
That puts the whole rent on one loaf. It is shared across all the loaves.
That is the total cost. Divide by the number of loaves.

questions.prompt: Why is average cost lowest where MC meets it?

choices.label: While MC is below the average each unit pulls it down; above it, each unit pulls it up.
Marginal cost is always lowest at that output.
Fixed costs vanish at that output.

acceptedIdeas: While MC is below the average each unit pulls it down; above it, each unit pulls it up.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A unit cheaper than the average pulls the average down, and a dearer unit pulls it up. The turning point is where they are equal.

hints: What does a unit that costs less than the average do to the average?
questions.onCorrect: A cheaper-than-average unit lowers the average, a dearer one raises it. The turn is where they meet.

misconceptions.feedback: Marginal cost keeps rising here. What matters is how it compares with the average.
Fixed cost never vanishes; it only gets spread thinner.

questions.prompt: Average total cost at that output, in pounds
hints: Put the output into the average cost formula.
Divide the rent by the output first.
Add the output to that.
questions.onCorrect: £20. At the lowest point average cost equals marginal cost, 2 × 10.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the output. Put it into ATC = 100/q + q.
That adds the rent per unit to twice the output. Use ATC = 100/q + q.

questions.prompt: The market price is £30 and the next unit's marginal cost is £34. Should the firm make that unit?

choices.label: No: it adds more cost than revenue.
Yes: the price is still positive.
Yes: fixed cost is already paid.

acceptedIdeas: No: it adds more cost than revenue.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The unit adds £30 of revenue and £34 of cost, so it lowers profit by £4.

hints: Compare the revenue the unit adds with the cost it adds.
questions.onCorrect: No. Each unit must add at least as much revenue as cost, or it lowers profit.

misconceptions.feedback: Positive revenue is not enough: the unit must add more revenue than it costs.
Fixed cost is the same either way, so it does not decide this unit. Compare its revenue with its marginal cost.

questions.prompt: The market price falls to £16. The firm still has TC = 100 + q² and MC = 2q. What is its profit at its best output, in pounds?
hints: First find the best output at the new price.
Work out revenue and total cost at that output.
Subtract cost from revenue. A loss is negative.
questions.onCorrect: −£36, a loss. It still beats shutting down, which would lose the whole £100 of rent.

misconceptions.feedback: That is revenue. Subtract total cost.
That is the cost. Subtract it from the revenue.
That subtracts only the rent. Variable cost counts too.

questions.prompt: A firm's total cost is TC = 80 + q². What is its average total cost at q = 8, in pounds?
hints: Find total cost at that output first.
Include the fixed cost.
Divide total cost by the output.
questions.onCorrect: £18. Total cost per unit, fixed cost included.

misconceptions.feedback: That shares only the fixed cost across the units. Variable cost counts too.
That is total cost. Divide by the output.
